topic: reviving a hand pump over a disused dug well: leathers, foot valve, priming and silt

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-2)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: sonda poziomu wody na tasmie

base: I am reviving an old hand pump over a dug well that has stood unused for years.
A stone trough beside it still holds water and the outlet channel runs into the garden.
A level probe on a marked tape tells me the water stands four metres down.
The hand pump draws nothing at all, though the handle moves freely through its whole stroke.
Should I start with the leathers, or is the foot valve the more likely culprit?
Start with the leathers, because a free handle usually means the piston seals nothing.
Dried leathers shrink away from the cylinder wall and let water slip straight past.
Pull the piston out and soak the leathers overnight in neatsfoot oil before judging them.
If they swell back to a snug fit, the foot valve may be perfectly sound.
The leathers swelled beautifully overnight and now grip the cylinder wall very firmly indeed.
The pump lifts water for about twenty strokes, then loses it and goes light again.
The level probe shows the water has not dropped, so the well itself is fine.
The stone trough fills slowly and then drains back down the pipe within a minute.
Does that point to the foot valve after all, or to a leak in the rising main?
It points to the foot valve, since water running back down is exactly what it prevents.
Grit under the seat holds the valve open a fraction and that is quite enough.
Lift the rising main and clean the seat, then check the leather flap for cracks.
A leak in the pipe itself would lose water steadily rather than only after stopping.
The foot valve seat had a stone chip wedged against it and the flap was hard.
I cleaned the seat and fitted a new leather flap cut from the same hide.
The pump now holds its prime overnight and lifts water within four or five strokes.
The water runs cloudy for the first minute, though, which I did not expect.
Cloudy water at the start means the well has silted while it stood unused.
Pump it hard for an hour a day and the cloudiness will clear within a week.
If it never clears, the pipe foot sits too near the bottom and stirs the silt.
Raising it half a metre usually solves that without losing any real depth of water.
A week of hard pumping cleared the water and it now runs bright from the spout.
I raised the pipe foot by half a metre anyway, since the well is deep enough.
The stone trough fills in about four minutes and holds its level overnight now.
Is the water safe for the garden, or should I have it tested before using it?
Use it on the garden freely, since surface water does no harm to growing plants.
Have it tested before anyone drinks it, because a dug well takes whatever the ground carries.
A shallow well near a yard is worth testing every spring rather than once.
Keep the cover tight in the meantime and stop leaves falling in through the gaps.
I fitted a new cover and the well stays clean even after a week of gales.
The pump squeaks badly on the upstroke now that everything else is working properly.
The noise seems to come from the handle pivot rather than from inside the cylinder.
Can I grease that pivot, or will grease find its way down into the water?
Grease the pivot freely, because it sits well above the cylinder and drains outward.
Use a thick waterproof grease and work it in with the handle right down.
Never oil anything below the packing, since that does reach the water eventually.
A pump greased twice a year will outlast everyone who ever pumps at it.
